Why it's theirs: Jo loves Kind of Blue (rated five out of five in their taste) and jazz history.
Facts: Miles Davis recorded Kind of Blue at Columbia's 30th Street Studio in New York across just two recording dates, March 2 and April 22, 1959. The band featured John Coltrane, Cannonball Adderley, Bill Evans, Paul Chambers, and Jimmy Cobb (with Wynton Kelly on Freddie Freeloader). Total time in the studio was about nine hours. Miles gave the musicians modal sketches and scales just hours before the tape rolled rather than standard full scores. Almost every master track on the record is a first complete take.
Point it lands on: Miles wanted absolute spontaneity over rehearsed perfection; when everyone knows their craft, the first honest take is often the best one.

stories.source: Bill Evans original 1959 liner notes to Kind of Blue
stories.text:
Why it's theirs: Jo loves Kind of Blue and deep jazz technique.
Facts: Bill Evans wrote the famous original liner notes on the back of Kind of Blue. He compared jazz improvisation to a traditional Japanese watercolor painting style (sumi-e). In that art, the painter draws with black water paint on thin stretched parchment: if a stroke hesitates, interrupts, or wavers, it breaks the paper or ruins the line. Erasures and corrections are physically impossible. Evans explained that Miles set up Kind of Blue under the same strict discipline: pure direct deed where deliberation cannot interfere.
Point it lands on: In lifting as in art: commit to the movement cleanly from the start without hesitating halfway through the rep.

Why it's theirs: Space history spare; Apollo near misses.

Rookie astronaut Alan Bean reached across the cabin and flipped the switch, instantly restoring telemetry and saving the flight.
Point it lands on: The legend of the 'steely-eyed missile man': calm recall under pressure beats panic every single time.

stories.topic: Space history: the missions, the people, the near misses
stories.title: The 1202 Computer Alarm on Apollo 11
stories.source: NASA Apollo 11 Mission Report: 1202 and 1201 Program Alarms
stories.text:
Why it's theirs: Jo loves space history, The Right Stuff, and near misses under high pressure.
Facts: During the Apollo 11 lunar descent on July 20, 1969, Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin were three minutes from touchdown when the computer flashed a 1202 alarm, followed by a 1201 alarm. The computer was overloaded with data because the rendezvous radar had been left in the wrong mode, stealing 15 percent of its processing capacity. Margaret Hamilton and her software engineering team at MIT had built asynchronous priority scheduling into the flight software. When overloaded, the machine dropped low-priority radar checks to keep calculating engine burns and attitude control without crashing. In Houston, twenty-six-year-old guidance officer Steve Bales verified with radar specialist Jack Garman that as long as the alarm wasn't continuous, they were 'go'.
Point it lands on: Smart systems drop the noise and protect the main priority when work piles up.

stories.topic: Jazz: the players, how the records were made, what to listen to next
stories.title: Kind of Blue Playing at the Wrong Speed
stories.source: The Making of Kind of Blue: Ashley Kahn / Sony Master Tapes (1992 re-release)
stories.text:
Why it's theirs: Jo loves Kind of Blue; explores a famous recording-speed mystery for the rest.
Facts: Myth or fact: For over thirty years after its 1959 release, every vinyl copy of Kind of Blue played Side One slightly sharp and slightly too fast. Fact: On March 2, 1959, the primary three-track tape machine at Columbia 30th Street Studio ran slightly slow due to a power motor issue. When the recorded tape was played back on standard-speed mastering decks to cut vinyl records, the pitch of 'So What', 'Freddie Freeloader', and 'Blue in Green' went sharp by about a quarter-tone. It wasn't corrected until 1992, when reissue engineer Mark Wilder found the safety three-track tape recorded simultaneously on a separate machine running at precise speed.
Point it lands on: Even an acknowledged masterpiece had a mechanical imperfection hidden in plain earshot for thirty-three years.

Knees bent at ninety degrees, arms up. Press lower back flat. Slowly extend opposite arm and leg while exhaling, then return and switch.

[count 3 go] [reps 8]
Reach long, lower back flat. [hold 4s]
Return, now switch sides. [hold 4s]
Keep the core braced tight. [hold 4s]
Two more reps, slow and controlled. [hold 4s]
Back to center, and feet down.

Sit upright or lie comfortably, letting shoulders drop.

Box breathing calms your system and settles your heart rate.

Breathe in for four. [pause 4s]
Hold it there. [pause 4s]
Exhale slowly. [pause 4s]
Hold empty. [pause 4s]

Open your eyes. How did that overall effort feel from one to ten, Jo? Glute bridges, push-ups, towel door rows, and core work are in the bank. Take that momentum into your day. Next time we train, we build from here. See you then.
